Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take qunut to mean obedience and steadfastness in it, while al-Sam'ani stresses persistence in devotion and al-Alusi links it to humility and submission. The readers differed on whether the verbs should be read in the feminine or masculine, and al-Tabari accepts both because the Arabs sometimes match the verb to the form of 'man' and sometimes to its meaning. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the doubling by the high rank of these women: their obedience is worth more, just as their sin is graver. As for the generous provision, most commentators, including al-Qurtubi and Ibn Juzayy, understand it as Paradise, while Ibn Atiyya mentions a possible worldly sense without deciding. Al-Razi notes that the generosity is attributed to the provision of the Hereafter because it comes without intermediaries. Some commentators extend the sense to every righteous believing woman.

This verse addresses the wives of the Prophet ﷺ and tells them that they are not like other women if they are conscious of God, since their rank depends on their piety. They are forbidden to speak to men in a soft, yielding tone, lest the one whose heart has a disease be tempted. The commentators differ on the meaning of this disease. Qatada understood it as hypocrisy, while Ikrima took it to mean desire for fornication, and al-Razi linked it to immorality. Some explain that the woman should avoid an overly tender manner when addressing strangers. They are instead told to speak in a proper, honest and clear way, free of any suggestion that could arouse desire or suspicion. Ibn Zayd understood the dangerous softness as that which enters men's hearts, and al-Mawardi lists several meanings of the word 'decent'. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the ruling extends beyond the Prophet's wives, since its reason is the fear of temptation. The verse is also presented as a lesson in piety rather than a restriction of status. The readings of the verb 'yatma'a' vary, and the scholars do not settle between them.

This verse, addressed to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, tells them to stay in their homes, not to display themselves as in the first jahiliyya, to establish prayer, to give zakat, and to obey God and His Messenger. The commentators explain that staying at home is a matter of dignity and composure; al-Tabari and others note that the two readings of the verb, with fatha or kasra on the qaf, carry the same meaning, al-Tabari preferring the kasra reading which derives from gravity and calm. On tabarruj, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Abi Najih understand swaying, coquetry and conceit in walking, while others define it as showing off adornments and charms. Opinions differ on the period of the first jahiliyya: between Adam and Noah according to al-Hakam, between Idris and Noah according to Ibn Abbas, in the time of Abraham according to al-Kalbi, or between Jesus and Muhammad according to al-Sha'bi. As to 'the people of the house', Ikrima, Muqatil and, in one transmission, Ibn Abbas, take it to mean the Prophet's wives alone, while Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Umm Salama and Anas include Ali, Fatima, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and Zayd ibn Arqam restricts it to those forbidden to receive charity. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that the wives are included, and that the verse also extends to others whom the Prophet joined to them. The 'rijs' means sin and moral impurity, and 'tathir' means preservation from wrongdoing.

This verse addresses the wives of the Prophet ﷺ and tells them to remember what is recited in their homes: the signs of Allah, meaning the Qur'an, and the wisdom, meaning the Sunna. It is both an exhortation and a reminder of a blessing, so that they give thanks to God for placing them in homes where revelation is recited. The commentators agree on this general sense. Al-Tabari and Qatada read it as a favour bestowed on the Prophet's wives, and al-Tabari explains that wisdom refers to what was revealed to the Prophet apart from the Qur'an, namely the Sunna. Al-Baghawi and Muqatil connect wisdom with the Qur'anic rulings and admonitions. Al-Razi understands the reminder as a call to know all duties and prohibitions in order to fulfil the one and avoid the other. For the closing words, 'Allah is Subtle and Aware', al-Tabari explains them as God's kindness toward them and His knowledge of their choice, while Ibn Kathir and others take them to mean God's gentleness toward His friends and His knowledge of all creation. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the word 'remember' may mean either to reflect upon or to recite. The commentators differ little on the core meaning, but more on the exact scope of wisdom and the nuances of the reminder.

This verse states that God has prepared forgiveness and a great reward for men and women who combine ten qualities. The commentators explain that the muslims are those who submit outwardly to God's command, the believers those who affirm it inwardly, the obedient those who devote themselves to worship with constancy, and the truthful those who are sincere in word, deed and intention. The patient endure hardship, keep to the duties and refrain from what is forbidden; the humble are those who are modest and reverent before God; the almsgivers give what is obligatory and what is voluntary; the fasting men and women observe the obligatory and voluntary fast; those who guard their chastity keep away from what is unlawful, and those who remember God often do so with heart and tongue. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others relate that the revelation answered the wives of the Prophet, or the women believers, who asked why they were not mentioned in the Qur'an as men were; al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi cite several accounts of the occasion. Commentators differ on the distinction between islam and iman: al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir hold that faith is narrower than submission, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that islam covers both faith and the acts of the limbs. Ibn Kathir explains humility as calm and modesty, while al-Mawardi lists several meanings including modesty, fear and prayer. Al-Alusi notes that abundant remembrance includes both the tongue and the heart. Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur point out that the conjunction waw joins the qualities for each category, and that the masculine pronoun in 'for them' gives precedence to men. The reward is the forgiveness of sins and Paradise.

This verse states that it is not fitting for a believing man or woman, once God and His Messenger have decided a matter, to hold a free choice that contradicts it; they must submit. Whoever disobeys God and His Messenger has clearly strayed. The commentators agree that the ruling is general: choice remains only where no decision has been made. On the occasion of revelation, the reports differ. Most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, say it concerns Zaynab bint Jahsh, whom the Prophet proposed for his freed slave Zayd ibn Haritha; she and her brother Abdullah at first refused, then accepted once the verse came down. Ibn Zayd instead links it to Umm Kulthum bint Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, who had offered herself to the Prophet and was given to Zayd. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that God's name is mentioned to magnify the Prophet's command, which is treated as God's own. Al-Qurtubi derives from the verse that the imperative form implies obligation, and holds that equality in marriage is judged by religion rather than lineage, a view he presents against the positions of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Ibn al-Qayyim sees in it the duty to submit to the judgment of God and His Messenger. As for the word 'straying', Ibn Kathir takes it as clear error, while al-Mawardi renders it as manifest injustice. All agree that the passage contains a general warning against disobeying God and His Messenger.

This verse concerns Zayd ibn Harithah, the freed slave and adopted son of the Prophet ﷺ, and Zaynab bint Jahsh. The commentators explain that God had blessed Zayd with Islam, and the Prophet had freed and adopted him. When Zayd consulted the Prophet about separating from his wife, the Prophet told him to keep her and fear God. The exegetes agree that what the Prophet concealed within himself, and what God revealed, was his marriage to Zaynab after her divorce, not merely an inclination toward her as some claim. His fear of what people might say is described as modesty and a wish to avoid giving rumours cause, not a fear that could harm him. All agree on the purpose of the marriage: to abolish the prohibition on marrying the former wife of an adopted son, and God's decree is bound to come to pass. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and others report that God Himself concluded the marriage, without a guardian, dowry or witnesses, and that Zaynab took pride in this over the Prophet's other wives. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur firmly reject the accounts of a passionate love of the Prophet for Zaynab, judging their chains weak or contrary to prophetic infallibility. The commentators connect this passage with the verse stating that Muhammad is not the father of any of your men but the Messenger of God and the seal of the prophets, his sons having died young. The verse also states that no believing man or woman has a choice once God and His Messenger have decided, and that fear of God takes precedence over fear of people.

The verse says there is no blame on the Prophet in what God permitted him, namely marrying Zaynab bint Jahsh after Zayd ibn Haritha, whom he had adopted, divorced her. The commentators agree that the phrase 'what God ordained for him' means what He made lawful for him. Al-Tabari, following Qatada, says God made it permissible. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain that 'the sunna of God' refers to the practice of earlier prophets, who also had several wives such as David and Solomon, and that God does not blame His prophets for what He has allowed them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read 'sunna' as a noun placed in the position of a verbal noun, and Ibn Atiyya gives other grammatical options. On the meaning of 'the decree of God', al-Tabari reports Ibn Zayd's view that it was written in God's knowledge before creation, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir say it is a settled command that must come to pass. Scholars differ on the reference of 'what was ordained': Muqatil and al-Kalbi say it is the marriage to Zaynab; al-Hasan says it is marriage without a dowry; al-Dahhak says it is more than four wives, a point raised because the Jews criticized the Prophet for his many marriages. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir mention that some link the verse to David's story, though this narrative is judged weak by several commentators. The common conclusion is that God's command is carried out and cannot be reversed.

This verse describes the prophets who came before Muhammad ﷺ: they convey the messages of Allah, fear Him, and fear no one but Him, and Allah suffices as a reckoner of their deeds. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, connect the verse to the preceding one and understand those who passed before as the prophets. They read it as an implicit reference to the Prophet ﷺ, who feared people's talk when he married Zaynab bint Jahsh after Zayd ibn Haritha divorced her. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir present the fear as the reason he was not to fear the criticism of others in lawful matters. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi state that the fear denied here is fear in delivering the message, while the fear mentioned in the previous verse concerned the hypocrites' talk. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan define khashya as fear mixed with reverence, whereas Ibn 'Ashur reads it as not letting worldly fear push the prophets away from their mission.

The commentators agree that the prophets were permitted by Allah to marry several wives, as David and Solomon did according to al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi, and that this involved no fault. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Kathir add that the abolition of adoption and its legal consequences forms part of the context. On the phrase "seal of the prophets", the commentators largely agree that it affirms that no prophet will come after Muhammad ﷺ, with al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir stressing this clearly.

This verse states that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is not the father of any of the men among you, meaning he was not the biological father of Zayd ibn Harithah, so the prohibition on marrying a adopted son's former wife does not apply to him. The commentators link the verse to the story of Zayd and Zaynab bint Jahsh. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir report that the Prophet's sons by Khadijah and Maria died as small children before reaching manhood, and Ibn Kathir notes that the negation does not concern grandsons. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand the denied fatherhood as legal fatherhood, carrying rights of marriage prohibition and inheritance, while holding that the Prophet is a spiritual father to the community in reverence, compassion and counsel. On the phrase Seal of the Prophets, all agree it means the last of the prophets; al-Tabari records the reading with a kasra (the one who sealed prophethood) and with a fatha (that by which the prophets were sealed). Several, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, explain that when Jesus descends before the end of time he will rule under Muhammad's law, which does not conflict with the seal. The verse closes by affirming God's complete knowledge of all things.

This verse commands believers to remember God abundantly, without limit, and to glorify Him at the beginning and end of the day. The commentators agree that remembrance involves the heart, the tongue and the limbs, and that abundance means persistence in every state. Ibn Abbas holds that God set no limit to this remembrance and excused no one from neglecting it except the person whose mind is overcome, while Mujahid says abundant remembrance means never forgetting God. As for glorifying Him at morning and evening, Qatada and al-Tabari take these as the dawn and afternoon prayers, al-Kalbi includes the noon, sunset and night prayers, al-Akhfash means the time between afternoon and night, and al-Baydawi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari take it as all parts of the day. God's blessing on the believers is explained by Abu al-Aliya as His praise, by al-Hasan as His mercy and by Ibn Jubayr as His forgiveness, while the angels' blessing is for Abu al-Aliya their supplication and for Muqatil their plea for forgiveness. The darkness is generally read as misguidance and disbelief, though some take it to mean the Fire and Paradise. The greeting on the day they meet Him is taken by some as God's peace upon them, by others as the angels' peace or that of the Angel of Death at the taking of souls, and by Qatada as the greeting the people of Paradise exchange. The generous reward is, for most, Paradise.

In this verse God commands the believers to remember Him often and to glorify Him at the beginning and end of the day. The commentators differ on what this glorification means. Al-Tabari and Qatada take it to mean the dawn and afternoon prayers, while al-Kalbi extends the evening period to the noon, afternoon, sunset and night prayers. Mujahid understands it as saying the formulas glorifying God, praising Him, declaring His oneness and His greatness, which even someone in a state of ritual impurity may recite. Ibn Abbas holds that remembrance has no fixed limit and that no one is excused from it except one whose mind is impaired, and Mujahid adds that it means never forgetting Him. All agree that God's prayer upon the believers is His mercy and praise, and that the angels' prayer is their intercession and supplication for them. Being brought out from darkness into light means being guided from error and disbelief to faith. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that God is merciful to the believers in this world through guidance and in the next through safety from terror. Their greeting on the day they meet God is, for Qatada and al-Tabari, the peace they exchange in Paradise, while al-Bara ibn Azib and Ibn Mas'ud relate it to the greeting of the Angel of Death at the taking of the soul, and others to the angels at the emergence from the graves. For all of them the great reward is Paradise. Some commentators connect the verse to the controversy over the Prophet's marriage to Zaynab, saying that the call to remembrance was meant to turn the believers away from such talk.

This verse says that Allah sends His blessing (salat) upon the believers, meaning His mercy and praise, and that His angels ask forgiveness for them, so that He brings them out of the darkness of misguidance, disbelief and disobedience into the light of guidance, faith and obedience, and that He is merciful to the believers. The commentators agree on the general sense. Most, such as al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Kathir, take Allah's salat to mean mercy, while Abu al-'Aliya and Ibn Zayd take it to mean praise, and others mean spreading a good reputation. For the angels' salat most say it is their supplication and plea for forgiveness on behalf of believers, and al-Zamakhshari explains that since their prayers are answered they are treated as if they themselves bring about mercy. al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi prefer a broader meaning covering mercy, forgiveness and care. On the darkness, Ibn Zayd explains it as misguidance, Muqatil as disbelief, al-Mawardi as hellfire versus paradise, while at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir include ignorance and sin. Ibn Kathir notes that the mercy applies in this world and the next. On the greeting on the day they meet Him, Qatada understands it as the believers greeting one another in Paradise, while others attribute it to the angels, to the Angel of Death, to the angels at the resurrection from the graves, or to the angels at the entry into Paradise. Most commentators identify the great reward as Paradise. Some report that the verse was revealed after the Companions said that the blessing mentioned in the previous verse on the Prophet was for him alone, so that they too might share in it.

This verse states that the greeting of the believers on the day they meet their Lord will be peace, and that God has prepared for them a generous reward, which is Paradise. The commentators read it in light of the verses before it, in which the believers are told to remember God abundantly and glorify Him morning and evening, and in which God's blessing and that of His angels bring them out of darkness into light. As to the meaning of "meeting", most take it to mean meeting God on the Day of Resurrection or upon entering Paradise. Others, such as al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and Ibn Mas'ud, reported by Ibn Kathir, understand it as meeting the Angel of Death, who greets the believer as he gives up his soul. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur favour that the peace comes from God Himself as an honour, while others hold that the angels give the good news of Paradise when people rise from their graves or enter it. Qatada and al-Tabari take it as the greeting the believers exchange among themselves. On the generous reward, all agree it is Paradise, which Ibn 'Ashur describes as precious in its value and its delights. Most commentators draw no legal ruling from this verse and limit themselves to explaining its meaning and its good news for the believers.

This verse presents the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as a witness over his community, a bearer of good news to those who believe and act righteously, a warner to those who reject faith, a caller to God by His permission, and a radiant lamp. The commentators broadly agree that witness means he testifies to having delivered the message to his people; al-Tabari and Qatada add that he also bears witness to the earlier prophets delivering theirs, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy extend this to witnessing people's deeds on the Day of Resurrection. As for calling to God, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Isa take it as calling to the testimony that there is no god but God, or to obedience; al-Hasan links the permission to action, and Yahya ibn Sallam to the Quran. On the lamp, Ibn Abbas and Qatada say it is the Quran, by which one is guided, whereas Ibn Shajara understands the Prophet himself; al-Zamakhshari explains that permission here means divine facilitation, since calling people to monotheism is very difficult. Ibn Ashur notes that good news is mentioned before warning because mercy predominates in the Prophet. On the great bounty, al-Kalbi understands a great reward, while Qatada and al-Kalbi say it is Paradise; al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi report that this part was revealed after the Companions asked what they would receive following the chapter of Victory. Regarding the command not to obey the disbelievers and hypocrites and to bear their harm, Mujahid and al-Tabari take it as patience and forbearance, while al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi consider it abrogated by the verse on fighting. All agree that trusting in God means that He suffices as protector.

God addresses His Prophet ﷺ as one sent to bear witness over his community, to bring good news to believers and warning to deniers, to call to God by His leave and facilitation, and as a lamp that gives light. The commentators agree that calling to God means affirming His oneness and abandoning the worship of others, and that the phrase 'by His leave' means by His command or by His facilitation. Ibn Abbas and Qatada take the illuminating lamp to be the Quran, while al-Naqqash and others take it to be the Prophet himself, some citing a verse of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr. Al-Zamakhshari explains that 'leave' is used figuratively for ease, since calling idolaters is so hard that it succeeds only through divine help. Al-Zajjaj and al-Farra' parse 'a lamp giving light' as coordinated with 'witness' or as an implied state. Ibn al-Qayyim argues that the Prophet is a lamp rather than the sun, since a lamp can kindle others without losing its light, and al-Razi applies the same idea to the Companions. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and others relate the report that the Prophet sent Ali and Mu'adh to Yemen to give good news. On the instruction to 'overlook their harm', some scholars regard it as abrogated by the verse on fighting, while others read it as a call to patience. All agree that the believers who receive the good news are those who believed and did righteous deeds, that the great bounty is Paradise, and that the prohibition on obeying disbelievers and hypocrites concerns whatever opposes God's command.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to a series describing the Prophet ﷺ: he is commanded to give good news to the believers that they will have from Allah a great bounty, which most of them understand as a great reward and Paradise. Al-Tabari takes the bounty to be the multiplication of reward for obedience, while Ibn Atiyya explains it as Paradise and what will be in it, relying on the verse of al-Shura that he considers its explanation. Al-Kalbi and Qatada speak of Paradise or a great reward, while al-Zamakhshari regards the bounty as an addition beyond the reward, and al-Razi holds that great and immense are close in meaning, the fact that it comes from Allah adding to its greatness.

Some relate an occasion of revelation: after the revelation of the chapter of Victory, the Companions asked what would be for them, and this verse was revealed. This account appears in al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi, transmitted from Jabir, Qatada and Ibn Abbas. The following verses, which forbid obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites and order enduring their harm while trusting in God, are read by most as patience in the face of abuse; al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan consider them abrogated by the verse of fighting.

The commentators take the "believers" to be those whose faith is firm and who act accordingly; Ibn Sa'di notes that when faith is mentioned alone it includes good deeds. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress that this promise encourages believers to obedience.

In this verse God instructs His Prophet ﷺ not to obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites, to bear their harm without retaliating, and to place his trust in God, who is sufficient as a guardian. The commentators identify the disbelievers as Meccans such as Abu Sufyan, Ikrima and Abu al-A'war al-Sulami, and the hypocrites as Abdullah ibn Ubayy, Abdullah ibn Sa'd and Tu'ma ibn Ubayriq, who reportedly asked the Prophet to show indulgence toward their idols. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi agree that not obeying means not heeding their proposals that contradict God's command and not abandoning the message. On the meaning of « leave their harm », opinions differ: al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take it as patience under abuse, while Ibn Abbas and al-Zajjaj take it as not repaying them in kind. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi note that the verbal noun can refer to the doer or the one harmed, so both readings remain possible. Several scholars, including al-Qurtubi, al-Baghawi and al-Sam'ani, report that the verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others do not accept this view. Tawakkul is understood as relying on God for help and protection, and wakil as the guardian who oversees the matter. Ibn Ashur links this verse to the preceding pairs of good tidings and warning.

This verse concerns a woman divorced after the marriage contract but before consummation. The commentators explain that if believers marry believing women and then divorce them before touching them, the husbands have no waiting period to count against them, and they should give them a provision and release them graciously without harm. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab hold that the provision applies to a woman for whom no dower was fixed, while one with a fixed dower receives only half of it; Ibn Kathir and others see the verse as abrogated by the verse of al-Baqara, whereas Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Ashur reconcile the two by specification. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi report that some regard the provision as obligatory, others as recommended, with Abu Hanifa among those who consider it recommended. All agree there is no waiting period after divorce before consummation. On seclusion (khalwa), Abu Hanifa, Umar, Ali and Ibn Mas'ud treat it as equivalent to consummation, while al-Shafi'i in his preferred view does not impose a waiting period on it alone. Scholars derive from the verse that a divorce cannot take effect before marriage, a point Malik and some Hanafis qualify for conditional cases. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan note that nikah here means the contract and that the word touching is a euphemism for intercourse.

This verse describes the provisions God granted His Prophet ﷺ regarding marriage and possession, as a favour and a relief. He was permitted to take as wives those whom he had given their dowries, those his right hand possessed from what God had granted him as spoils, his paternal and maternal cousins who had emigrated with him, and a believing woman who gave herself to him without a dowry, if he wished to marry her, a privilege reserved for him over the other believers. The commentators explain that these conditions, such as the dowry and the emigration, were not necessary for the validity of the marriage, but were meant to direct him to what was most excellent. Some understand emigration as conversion to Islam. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report the account of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, who said she was not permitted to him because she had not emigrated, while others, such as al-Razi, hold that the emigration condition was abrogated. On the woman who gave herself to the Prophet, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid say that no such woman was ever with him, while the majority hold that there were several, and names mentioned include Maymuna bint al-Harith, Zaynab bint Khuzayma, Umm Sharik and Khawla bint Hakim. On God's words, 'We know what We have prescribed for them concerning their wives,' the commentators apply it to the rules for other believers: no more than four wives, the presence of a guardian and witnesses, and a dowry. Regarding 'Women are not lawful to you after this,' Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'isha regard it as abrogated, while al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin consider it binding, God having rewarded the wives who chose Him by limiting the Prophet to them. The verse closes with God's forgiveness and mercy, which remove any hardship from the Prophet in these matters.

The verse grants the Prophet ﷺ the discretion to defer the turn of whichever wife he wishes, to take to himself whom he wills, and to recall one he had set aside, without blame upon him. The commentators read the deferring and taking in several ways. Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Kathir in one report, understand divorce and retention; al-Hasan understands leaving off marrying some women while marrying others; Mujahid understands setting aside without divorce and then taking back. The majority, including Qatada, Abu Razin, Ibn Zayd, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, hold that it concerns the sharing of nights among his wives: God gave him the choice in what had been obligatory, and he nonetheless kept sharing out of care for their hearts. Al-Sha'bi and Zayd ibn Aslam relate it to the women who offered themselves to the Prophet, and al-Tabari reconciles the views by reading the verse generally. On the phrase that this is closer to comforting their eyes, Qatada says that when they know the ruling comes from God they are content, while Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid say they know he may take back the one he set aside. On the words that no women are lawful to him after this, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan restrict it to the nine wives who chose God and His messenger; Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Ikrima take it as following the categories already named; a report from Aisha says the restriction was lifted before his death, which others dispute. The Prophet took no new wife after the revelation and divorced no one in order to marry another.

This verse speaks to the Prophet ﷺ: after his wives chose God, His Messenger and the Hereafter, he may not take other wives, nor divorce one of them to replace her, even if another's beauty pleases him, except what his right hand possesses. Commentators see in it a reward and honour for the wives for their choice. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari (in one of his views) conclude that the Prophet was restricted to these wives, and that nine was for him what four is for other believers. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Ikrima and Abu Razin explain that the verse refers to the categories of women named in the previous verse, paternal and maternal cousins and women who offered themselves. Mujahid understands it as forbidding non-Muslim women. Others, including 'A'isha, Umm Salama, 'Ali and, in one report, Ibn 'Abbas, hold that the verse was abrogated and that marriage was permitted to him before his death. Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin hold that it remains in force. On replacing wives, al-Dahhak sees a prohibition on divorcing to substitute, while Ibn Zayd reports a pre-Islamic custom of exchanging wives, which Tabari and others reject. Most note that beauty does not justify substitution, and that concubines remain permitted. Opinions differ on the non-Muslim slave-woman. God watches over all things.

This verse instructs believers not to enter the Prophet's homes unless they are given leave, and to enter only when invited to a meal, without arriving early to wait for the food to be ready. Once they have eaten, they should leave rather than linger in conversation, since such lingering troubles the Prophet, who out of modesty would not ask them to go, while God is not shy of the truth. It also directs that anything requested from the Prophet's wives be asked from behind a screen, which the verse says is purer for both hearts. It closes by forbidding harm to the Messenger and marriage to his widows after his death, calling this a grave matter in God's sight. The commentators report that the verse was revealed in connection with the wedding feast of Zaynab bint Jahsh, when some guests stayed on long after the meal. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree on this occasion, and several also report the episode involving Umar and the veil, which Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate. Al-Qurtubi and al-Razi note that the ban on marrying his widows applies firmly, but disagree on those he divorced before consummation or those who chose God and His Messenger. Ibn Kathir stresses that the prohibition on harming the Prophet is absolute. Al-Shinqiti argues that the veil applies to all women, while other scholars limit it to the Prophet's wives.

This verse warns that God knows whatever people utter openly or conceal in their hearts, and will call them to account for it. The commentators link it to what precedes it, namely the verses of the veil and the rules for entering the Prophet's houses, so it serves as a warning to anyone who speaks or harbours an intention that would hurt the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the matter in question is the intention to marry the Prophet's wives after his death, a remark attributed to a companion whose name varies across the reports: Ibn Kathir and others name Talha ibn Ubayd Allah, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers that attribution unsound for Talha. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read the word 'thing' as general, covering this intention and any other act that offends the Prophet. Al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi focus more on what is concealed within the self. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan note that the prohibition on marrying the Prophet's widows is agreed upon, and that the disagreement concerns a wife divorced after consummation during his lifetime. Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as a comprehensive exhortation reminding believers that God observes every inner and outer state. Most exegetes stress the totality of God's knowledge and see the wide scope of the phrasing as intensifying the warning.

This verse states that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, and believing women more generally, commit no sin by not veiling before the relatives it names: fathers, sons, brothers, sons of brothers and sons of sisters, as well as before other women and the slaves they own. God then commands them to be mindful of Him. Al-Tabari and Qatada understand this as permission to go unveiled before these people, while Mujahid takes it to mean removing the outer cloak and showing adornment, a reading also favoured by Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi. As for the omission of the paternal and maternal uncles, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir explain that they stand in the place of parents, and the uncle is even called a father elsewhere in the Quran, whereas al-Sha'bi and Ikrima suggest that they might describe the woman to their sons, a reason al-Alusi finds unconvincing. Commentators differ on the word women: al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Juzayy take it to mean believing women, while others include all women. On the slaves, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab restricts the term to female slaves, whereas others include male and female slaves, and al-Qurtubi notes that a mukatab slave who can pay for his freedom is not exempt from the veil, as Umm Salama practised. The verse closes with a warning that God is a witness over all things, including what people conceal and what they reveal.

In this verse Allah tells us that He and His angels honour the Prophet ﷺ, and then commands the believers to pray upon him and to greet him with peace. The commentators explain Allah's prayer in several ways: Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliya take it as praise and exaltation before the angels, al-Hasan and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah take it as mercy, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr as forgiveness. The angels' prayer is supplication and asking forgiveness for him. They agree that the command to pray upon the Prophet means saying: O Allah, send Your blessings upon Muhammad and his family as You sent them upon Abraham and his family. They differ on the wording and details. Al-Shafi'i holds that the blessing upon the Prophet is obligatory in the final tashahhud and that the prayer is invalid without it, while Malik and Abu Hanifa consider it a strongly recommended sunna whose omission does not invalidate the prayer. Scholars also differ on whether it is obligatory each time his name is mentioned: some require it once in each gathering, some once in a lifetime, and others consider it recommended. As for the command to greet him with peace, some read it as the greeting and the prayer for safety, while others read it as submission to his commands. A hadith says the best wording is the one he taught his companions, though its versions differ in some words. The next verse warns that those who harm Allah and His Messenger through disbelief, insult or denial are cursed by Allah in this world and the next. It also warns those who hurt believing men and women without cause, which the commentators describe as slander and manifest sin.

This verse states that those who harm Allah and His Messenger are cursed by Allah in this world and the Hereafter, and that a humiliating punishment awaits them. The commentators explain the verb 'to harm' in several ways. Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes take it to refer to polytheists, Jews and Christians who attribute a son or a partner to God and describe Him unworthily, such as the Jewish saying 'the hand of God is chained' or the Christian claim that the Messiah is the son of God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi also cite the hadith in which God says that the son of Adam insults time. Harming the Prophet ﷺ is understood by them as harm by words, such as the labels poet, sorcerer or madman, and by deeds, such as the breaking of his tooth at Uhud, or the criticism of his marriage to Safiyya bint Huyayy, reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur hold that the word is used figuratively for God and literally for the Prophet. Al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari also mention idolatry and the making of images, reported from 'Ikrima, or an ellipsis meaning the friends of God. The next verse, according to the commentators, concerns harming believing men and women without any cause, which is slander and manifest sin. They report several occasions of revelation: hypocrites who harassed 'Ali, libertines who pursued women, and the slander affair concerning 'A'isha. The exegetes agree that offending the Prophet is especially grave, and that the protection owed to believers extends to every unjustified harm.

This verse states that those who harm believing men and women without their having earned it have borne a calumny and a manifest sin. The commentators explain that harm may be done by speech or by deed. Al-Tabari, followed by Ibn Kathir, understands the verb yu'dhun as attacking believers with words, belittling them and accusing them falsely, and he reports from Mujahid that it means to stop them and slander them. Al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi stress that the harm is inflicted without any offence on the victim's part. Ibn Kathir adds that the clear calumny is to attribute to believers what they did not do, and he cites a hadith that an honest mention of someone's faults is backbiting while a false one is slander. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the phrase without what they earned excludes legitimate punishments such as the prescribed penalty or discipline, which belong to the authorities rather than private persons. Al-Razi holds that calumny concerns speech only, whereas harm may also be physical, such as beating or seizing property, and so he takes the verse to refer chiefly to verbal harm. On the occasion of revelation the reports differ: Muqatil links it to hypocrites who harassed Ali, al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak to adulterers who followed women in the streets of Medina, and al-Dahhak also to the slander concerning A'isha. Al-Qurtubi also mentions the report of 'Umar, who was frightened by this verse. The commentators agree that harming believers without a just cause is forbidden.

The verse instructs the Prophet, peace be upon him, to tell his wives, his daughters and the believing women to draw their jalabib over themselves, so that they will be recognized as free women and not be harassed. The commentators explain that the jilbab is a garment wider than the khimar, worn over other clothing, and they differ on how it should be drawn. Ibn Abbas and Ubayda al-Salmani hold that the woman should cover her face, leaving only one eye visible, a view also reported by al-Tabari. Another report from Ibn Abbas and Qatada says she should fold it over the forehead and down over the nose, so that the eyes may show but the chest and most of the face are covered. Al-Hasan speaks of covering half the face, and al-Sudi of covering one eye, the forehead and one side of the face. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur emphasize that the purpose is to distinguish free women from slave women, who dressed differently and were not to be mistaken for them. They add that the aim is not to identify the individual woman, but to set her apart from a servant. The commentators relate that men of ill repute lurked in the streets of Medina at night, pursuing servants and leaving alone those who were visibly veiled, which prompted the revelation. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that modesty both protects women from slander and guards them from temptation. Ibn Kathir and others observe that the closing words, God is Forgiving and Merciful, refer to past lapses made before the command was given. Al-Alusi reports that Umar struck female slaves who veiled themselves, and that some jurists did not require veiling of slaves.

This verse warns the hypocrites, those with sickness in their hearts, and the spreaders of rumours in Madinah: if they do not desist, God will give His Messenger power over them until they are expelled or destroyed, cursed and seized wherever they are found. Commentators agree that the three descriptions may refer to overlapping groups. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi explain the verb 'nughriyannaka' as giving you power over them, or inciting you against them, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand it as a command to fight them and drive them out. As for the sickness in the heart, 'Ikrima, Shahr ibn Hawshab and al-Tabari take it to mean fornication and lust, al-Suddi means hypocrisy, al-Kalbi means harming the Muslims, and Ibn 'Ashur means hypocrisy or wavering in faith. The rumour-mongers, according to Qatada and al-Tabari, spread news of defeat or the death of expeditions to break the hearts of believers. Scholars differ on whether the threat was carried out. Some say the hypocrites desisted, others that they did not desist and the threat was never executed. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn 'Uthaymin lean toward the first view. The phrase 'except for a little' is read as a short period or a small number, depending on the commentator. Commentators conclude that God's established way with earlier peoples is that whoever openly persists in hypocrisy is banished or killed, and that this way does not change.

This verse states God's threat against the hypocrites, those with sickness in their hearts, and the rumour-mongers in Medina if they do not desist. The plain meaning is that God will set His Prophet against them, giving him power over them or urging him on, so that they will stay in the city only briefly, cursed wherever they are found, seized and killed. Ibn Abbas understood the incitement as granting power over them, Qatada as urging him to restrain them or hold them to account, and al-Suddi as informing him about them. Most commentators hold that the three categories often refer to closely related groups among the hypocrites. Al-Tabari, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir identify those with sickness in their hearts as adulterers and seekers of illicit desire, Qatada ties the sickness to lust for fornication, and al-Kalbi and Salama ibn Kuhayl speak more broadly of people of immorality. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi take the three descriptions as referring to one and the same group. Qatada and al-Zamakhshari explain the rumour-mongering as spreading reports of defeat among the Prophet's expeditions, while Ibn Abbas says it meant seeking to stir up strife. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir note that the hypocrites may have desisted and so the threat was not carried out, whereas al-Shawkani holds that the incitement never took place, and Ibn Uthaymin judges it likelier that they stopped out of fear. Commentators explain that the seizing and killing are a command, that cursed describes a state or is a term of reproach, and that God's established way with earlier peoples does not change.

This verse states that what God threatened against the hypocrites and the rumour-mongers in Medina, namely that the Prophet ﷺ would be empowered against them and that they would be expelled or seized and killed wherever found, is God's established way with earlier peoples, and that no one can change it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as applying to hypocrites who persist after being warned, who are then cursed and killed. Al-Suddi and Qatada take it as a rule of legal punishment for fornication, or that whoever openly shows hypocrisy is banished, or that one killed justly has no blood-money; Yahya ibn Salam says whoever openly shows polytheism is killed. Muqatil and Ibn Juzayy suggest it may refer to the unbelievers killed or captured at Badr. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the threat may have been carried out, or that the hypocrites ceased their conduct and it was never enforced, and they recall the Prophet expelling the hypocrites from the mosque after the revelation of Bara'a. Al-Razi explains that change applies only to abrogable rulings, not to deeds and reports. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the negation is general, covering past, present and future peoples. All agree that God's way cannot be altered, but they differ on who exactly is meant and on the details of the punishment.

People ask the Prophet ﷺ when the Hour will come, and God orders him to answer that knowledge of it belongs to Him alone, and that He has not revealed it even to an angel or a prophet. Al-Tabari explains that "what will make you know" means "what will inform you," and that the Hour is near, a view shared by al-Sam'ani, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, who cite the verse "the Hour has drawn near." According to al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, the questioners were polytheists mocking and hurrying the matter, and Jews testing the Prophet, since its timing was concealed in the Torah; the reply warns the hasty and silences the challengers. As for the masculine form of "near," al-Zajjaj and Abu Hayyan explain it as an adverb of time, as an implied "thing" or "day," or because "Hour" has a non-real feminine; Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu al-Su'ud allow it to be an adjective. Al-Qurtubi cites the hadith "I was sent, and the Hour, like these two," and Ibn 'Ashur notes that the askers differed: mockers, believers wishing to know, and Jews testing the Prophet. The commentators agree that the passage belongs to a context of threatening the hypocrites and the mockers, and that disbelievers are cursed in this world and the next. Al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that what truly matters is preparing for the Hour rather than knowing its date.

This verse states that God has banished the disbelievers from His mercy and has prepared for them in the Hereafter a blazing fire, in which they will remain forever, finding neither a protector to guard them nor a helper to rescue them from punishment. The commentators explain the curse as expulsion and distance from mercy, and the sa'ir as a fire that is kindled and blazing. They agree that the abode is everlasting and that no one can relieve these people of it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the verse describes the condition of the unbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when their faces will be turned over in the Fire and they will wish they had obeyed God and His Messenger. Al-Razi notes that the face is singled out for its honour, and that no other limb can shield it. The same authors report that the unbelievers will complain that they obeyed their leaders and elders, who led them astray, and will ask that their punishment be doubled. On the reading of the phrase la'nan kabiran, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer the majority reading with the letter tha, kathiran, which suggests repeated cursing, whereas Asim and Ibn Amir read it with the letter ba, kabiran. The commentators take the sadat to be the leaders and chiefs, Tawus taking them to be the notables, and the kubara to be the scholars or the elders. Few exegetes draw any legal ruling from this passage, their attention falling mainly on the description of the punishment and the shared responsibility of those who followed.

This verse states that God has removed the disbelievers from His mercy and prepared for them a blazing fire, in which they will remain forever, finding neither a protector nor a helper. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di read it as describing a punishment without end, from which no one can rescue them. Al-Razi explains that a person being punished is freed only by a friend who intercedes for him or a helper who drives the punishment away, and neither will be available to them. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take the protector to be one who guards them and the helper to be one who repels the torment, while Ibn Sa'di understands the protector as one who grants what they ask for. Al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti explain khalidin as a state that has been decreed in advance, whereas Ibn 'Ashur treats it as a circumstantial clause. Al-Nasafi uses the verse to refute the Jahmiyya, who claimed that Paradise and Hell would eventually perish. Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Sha'rawi stress that the word abadan, used for the eternity of Hell in only three verses, clearly confirms its permanence, and that sinful believers may still find intercessors, something denied to the disbelievers. There is broad agreement on the endlessness of the punishment and the absence of any helper, while the commentators differ on the precise meaning of the two terms wali and nasir.

This passage describes the fate of the disbelievers in the Hereafter. The commentators explain that God has cast them away from His mercy and prepared for them a blazing fire, where they will remain forever with no protector or helper. The verse then portrays the day their faces are turned over in the Fire, when they will cry out: "If only we had obeyed Allah and the Messenger!" The commentators agree that this regret will be of no use, since the time for action has passed. They differ, however, on the meaning of the turning. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Juzayy and most exegetes take it as the faces being turned from side to side, like meat roasting over a fire, or changing state from one moment to the next. Ibn 'Ashur adds that it may refer to the faces changing colour under the scorching flame. The face is singled out because it is the noblest part of the body, and some say it stands for the whole person. As for the "chiefs and elders" whom the damned blame for leading them astray, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir identify them as the notables and rulers, Tawus includes the scholars, and Muqatil thinks of the nobles who fed the army at Badr. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi hold that the meaning is general and covers all leaders of misguidance. On the readings, al-Tabari prefers "la'nan kathiran" with the letter tha, while 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "kabiran" with ba. Abu 'Ali prefers tha, since multiplicity suits repeated curses. Finally, commentators note that the long alif at the end of "al-rasula" and "al-sabila" is a pausal alif used at the end of verses.

This passage recounts the words of the people of the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, when their faces are turned over in the flames and they lament not having obeyed God and His Messenger. Verse 67 records their complaint against their leaders and great ones: they say they obeyed their masters and elders, who led them astray from the path. The commentators agree that the sayyid and kubara are the leaders of disbelief and the guides to error who taught them unbelief and made it attractive. Ibn Abbas and Tawus understood the masters as the nobles and the elders as the scholars or senior men, while Abu Usama took them to be the commanders, and Qatada described them as the chiefs in polytheism. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil report that the verse concerned men of Quraysh who fed the troops at Badr, but most exegetes take its meaning as general. On the reading, the singular sadatana is the common one, while Ibn Amir and Yaqub read the plural sadatana, and al-Tabari considers the singular the established reading. For the request of double punishment, Qatada explained it as the torment of this world and the next, while others took it as the punishment of disbelief and that of misleading others. For the curse "a great curse", the readings kathiran (many) and kabiran (great) both occur, and the exegetes regard them as close in meaning. The overall lesson drawn is that blind imitation does not remove responsibility, and that followers and leaders share the punishment.

This verse records what the disbelievers will say on the Day of Resurrection, when their faces are turned over in the Fire. They wish they had obeyed God and His Messenger, then complain of their leaders and great ones whom they followed and who led them astray from the path. They then ask God to double the punishment of these leaders and to curse them with a great curse. The commentators broadly agree on the plain sense: the leaders should receive twice the punishment of the followers, because they went astray and led others astray, and the prayer expresses deep regret. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the 'sadat' are the notables, rulers or princes, while the 'kubara' are the scholars or elders, following Tawus; al-Mawardi reports three opinions on the first term and two on the second. As for the double punishment, Qatada takes it to mean the torment of this world and of the next, while others, including al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and al-Shawkani, take it to mean the punishment for disbelief and the punishment for misguiding others. On the reading, Asim and Ibn Amir read 'kabiran' with a ba, meaning great or severe, while most readers read 'kathiran' with a tha, meaning numerous; Abu Hatim, Abu Ubayd and al-Nahhas prefer the latter, citing other verses of cursing. Ibn Ashur notes that their excuse of having followed their leaders is turned back against them, since they followed them blindly. Al-Zamakhshari observes that the added final alif serves the rhyme and marks a pause.

In this verse God commands the believers not to harm the Prophet ﷺ as the Children of Israel harmed their prophet Moses, whom God then cleared of what they said about him; Moses was honoured with a high standing before God. The commentators agree that the verse forbids hurting the Prophet ﷺ by word or deed, and that doing so is a serious sin. Regarding what the Children of Israel accused Moses of, opinions differ. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayra, cited by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, report that they accused him of a swelling of the testicles, leprosy or some defect, because he covered himself so much out of modesty; one day, while he bathed alone, a stone carried off his clothes, and they saw him free of any defect. Ali ibn Abi Talib, cited by al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi, reports that they accused him of killing his brother Aaron, and that the angels carried the body past their assemblies to show he had not been killed. Abu al-'Aliya, cited by al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, tells of the woman whom Qarun hired to accuse him. Al-Tabari holds that no single account is more correct than the others and that all may be accepted. According to al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari, the harm may also refer to other forms of abuse. As for the Prophet ﷺ, the commentators say the verse may refer to the affair of Zayd and Zaynab or to a remark about the distribution of spoils, and they cite his saying: May God have mercy on Moses, he was harmed more than this and he was patient. On the meaning of wajih, al-Hasan takes it as one whose supplications are answered, Ibn Zayd as one who is accepted, and Qutrub as one of high rank. The verse closes by calling for the fear of God and for speech that is upright, which the commentators say makes deeds sound, forgives sins, and leads to a great success.

This verse commands believers to fear God, meaning to avoid disobedience and fulfil their duties, and to speak in a upright, sound manner (sadid). Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the word as straight, just, truthful or correct speech, while Mujahid understands it as rectitude; Ikrima, and in one report Ibn Abbas, take it to mean the declaration that there is no god but God. Ibn Kathir holds that all these meanings are true, since the word encompasses them. The reward mentioned is that God will set right the believers' deeds and forgive their sins. Al-Tabari and al-Baydawi take this as God guiding them to good deeds, whereas Ibn Abbas and al-Baghawi take it as the acceptance of their good deeds, and al-Mawardi notes both readings. Al-Zamakhshari explains that this verse complements the previous one: the first forbids harming the Prophet, while this one calls for guarding the tongue, so that prohibition and command reinforce each other. Ibn Kathir states that whoever obeys God and His Messenger achieves a great triumph, namely protection from the Fire and entry into lasting bliss. Al-Baydawi adds that such a person lives praiseworthy in this world and happy in the next. Qatada and Muqatil link the command to the affair of Zaynab and Zayd, while others read it as a general rule.

This verse calls on believers to fear God and to speak in a sound, upright way. If they do so, God will set their deeds right and forgive their sins, and whoever obeys God and His Messenger has achieved a great triumph. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and most exegetes understand sadid as truthful, just and correct speech, while al-Mawardi lists six meanings, including truth, correctness, speech whose outward matches its inward, and words sincerely intended for God's sake, and he also mentions reconciling disputing parties, drawing on the image of an arrow aimed true at its target. Ikrima takes it to mean the testimony that there is no god but God, while Ibn Kathir holds that all these explanations are correct. Muqatil and Qatada connect the verse to the affair of Zaynab and Zayd, warning against attributing to the Prophet what is unfitting. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan read the verse as reinforcing what precedes it: after the prohibition on harming the Prophet, believers are told to guard their tongues. On the setting right of deeds, Ibn Abbas, Muqatil and al-Nasafi take it to mean that good deeds are accepted, whereas al-Tabari and al-Baydawi take it to mean guidance toward righteous action. Al-Jaza'iri explains the great triumph as deliverance from the Fire and entry into Paradise.

This verse says that God offered the trust, meaning the religious obligations together with the reward and punishment attached to them, to the heavens, the earth and the mountains. They refused to carry it and feared its consequences, but man took it up, though he is wrongdoing to himself and ignorant of the outcome. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Qatada, and most exegetes, understand the trust as the obligations and acts of obedience God imposed on His servants. They hold that the offering was a choice rather than a compulsion, and that the refusal came from fear of falling short rather than from disobedience. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir consider these views close to one another, since they all return to religious responsibility and acceptance of commands and prohibitions, and the examples given by the early scholars, such as prayer, fasting, ritual washing after impurity and guarding one's chastity, are illustrations of that single meaning. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan report other opinions: the trust may be entrusted goods, reason, or the proofs of God's lordship, and offering it to the heavens and earth may mean offering it to their angels, as al-Hasan said. As for the man in the verse, Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak took him to be Adam, al-Suddi Qabil, al-Hasan the disbeliever and hypocrite, and Tha'lab the whole human race. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the offering and the refusal as an image meant to convey how heavy the responsibility is. The verse then continues with the punishment of hypocrites and idolaters and the forgiveness granted to believers.

This verse explains that God offered the trust, meaning the duty to obey Him, perform the obligations and avoid the forbidden, to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, who refused to bear it out of fear of its consequences, so man took it up, though he is wrongdoing to himself and ignorant of the outcome. The commentators explain that this bearing of the trust leads to judgement: God punishes hypocrite men and women who showed faith while hiding disbelief, and the polytheist men and women, and He turns in mercy to believing men and women, for God is forgiving and merciful. Most exegetes agree that the trust means the religious duties of the revealed law. Ibn Mas'ud took it first to mean material trusts such as deposits, while Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu al-Darda' included guarding chastity and the ritual bath after major impurity. Ibn Kathir and others note that these views do not contradict each other, since all return to moral responsibility and accepting commands on condition of carrying them out. On how the trust was offered, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, with al-Baydawi, report a real offer, sometimes with a grant of perception to created things, and a choice rather than an obligation. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Sha'rawi read it as a figure of speech stressing the trust's weight. On the identity of man, the majority, including al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi, say Adam, al-Suddi says Qabil, al-Hasan says the disbeliever and hypocrite, and Tha'lab says all humankind. As for the lam in 'to punish', many treat it as the lam of consequence rather than purpose: punishment is the outcome of bearing the trust. Ar-Razi explains that punishment is placed before pardon because breaking a trust makes one liable, whereas keeping it does not automatically earn reward. Al-Hasan read 'wa yatubu' in the nominative, making it an independent clause. For most, repentance here means pardon granted to those who fell short yet remained believers.
